simple: a number stored as "this many marks, on a scoop of this size".
analogy: Amara picks a scoop, then reads the nearest mark.
precise: a value (−1)^s × m × 2^e, where the significand m has a fixed number p of binary digits and the exponent e lies in a fixed range; the binary point "floats" with e.
source: S1 of F0-73 (IEEE, "IEEE Standard for Floating-Point Arithmetic" (IEEE Std 754; tier 1; registry 4.1) — title only, not opened); S2 of F0-73 (David Goldberg, "What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic" (ACM Computing Surveys, 1991; tier 5; registry 4.1) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the agreed 32-bit and 64-bit layouts for floating-point numbers; C++ float and double use them on this course's machine.
analogy: two standard scoop sets that every kitchen buys from the same catalogue.
precise: binary32: 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, 23 fraction bits, precision p = 24; binary64: 1, 11 and 52 bits, p = 53. On this build machine std::numeric_limits<float>::is_iec559 is 1 and digits is 24 (53 for double).
source: S1 of F0-73 (IEEE, "IEEE Standard for Floating-Point Arithmetic" (IEEE Std 754; tier 1; registry 4.1) — title only, not opened); R2 of F0-73 (lab run in this build: spacing.cpp) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the digits of the number, without its size.
analogy: the marks on the chosen scoop.
precise: for a normal number the significand is 1.f in binary: a hidden leading 1 followed by the stored fraction field f (23 bits in binary32). Older texts say "mantissa".
source: S1 of F0-73 (IEEE, "IEEE Standard for Floating-Point Arithmetic" (IEEE Std 754; tier 1; registry 4.1) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the power of two, stored with a constant added so that it is never negative.
analogy: the scoop's number in the drawer, counted from the smallest.
precise: in binary32 the 8-bit field E stores e + 127 for normal numbers (E = 1 … 254); E = 0 and E = 255 are reserved for zeros/subnormals and infinities/NaN.
source: S1 of F0-73 (IEEE, "IEEE Standard for Floating-Point Arithmetic" (IEEE Std 754; tier 1; registry 4.1) — title only, not opened); R1 of F0-73 (lab run in this build: bits.cpp) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a tiny number below the smallest normal one, stored with fewer significant digits.
analogy: the smallest scoop, read with some of its marks covered up.
precise: E = 0 and f ≠ 0 encodes 0.f × 2^(−126) in binary32; subnormals fill the gap between 0 and 2^(−126) with equal spacing 2^(−149) ("gradual underflow").
source: S1 of F0-73 (IEEE, "IEEE Standard for Floating-Point Arithmetic" (IEEE Std 754; tier 1; registry 4.1) — title only, not opened); R1 of F0-73 (lab run in this build: bits.cpp) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the gap between a float and the next bigger float.
analogy: the distance between two neighbouring marks on the scoop you are using.
precise: for a binary32 normal number with exponent e, ulp = 2^(e−23); it doubles at each power of two. Measured here with std::nextafter.
source: D1 of F0-73 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); R2 of F0-73 (lab run in this build: spacing.cpp) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how far 1 is from the next number up.
analogy: the gap between marks on the "1 cup" scoop.
precise: ε = 2^(1−p): 2^(−23) ≈ 1.19 × 10^(−7) for float and 2^(−52) ≈ 2.22 × 10^(−16) for double, as std::numeric_limits<T>::epsilon() printed in run R2. Do not confuse it with the unit roundoff u = ε/2 of F0-74.
source: B2 of F0-73 (ISO/IEC JTC1/SC22/WG21, working draft of the C++ standard (ISO/IEC 14882; tier 1; registry 4.1) — title only, not opened); R2 of F0-73 (lab run in this build: spacing.cpp) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

term: Round to nearest, ties to even
simple: the default rule: pick the closest float; on an exact tie, pick the one whose last bit is 0.
analogy: read the nearest mark; if the level is exactly halfway, always choose the "even" mark so that ties do not all lean one way.
precise: the default rounding-direction attribute of IEEE 754 for binary formats; every basic operation (+, −, ×, ÷, square root) returns the exact result rounded by this rule.
source: S1 of F0-73 (IEEE, "IEEE Standard for Floating-Point Arithmetic" (IEEE Std 754; tier 1; registry 4.1) — title only, not opened); S2 of F0-73 (David Goldberg, "What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic" (ACM Computing Surveys, 1991; tier 5; registry 4.1) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: special patterns meaning "too big to store" and "not a number at all".
analogy: a note in the recipe saying "overflowed the bucket" or "this step made no sense".
precise: E = 255 with f = 0 encodes ±∞; E = 255 with f ≠ 0 encodes NaN; a NaN compares unequal to everything, including itself.
source: S1 of F0-73 (IEEE, "IEEE Standard for Floating-Point Arithmetic" (IEEE Std 754; tier 1; registry 4.1) — title only, not opened); R1 of F0-73 (lab run in this build: bits.cpp) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the largest relative error one rounding can make.
analogy: the most a single levelled scoop can be off, as a fraction of the scoop.
precise: u = 2^(−p) for round to nearest in a binary format of precision p: 2^(−24) ≈ 5.96 × 10^(−8) for float (run R1) and 2^(−53) ≈ 1.11 × 10^(−16) for double; u is half the machine epsilon of F0-73.
source: B1 of F0-74 (Nicholas J. Higham, "Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms" (SIAM; tier 3) — title only, not opened); R1 of F0-74 (lab run in this build: roundoff.cpp) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: every basic operation gives the exact answer times a number very close to 1.
analogy: each scoop holds "the right amount, plus or minus a tiny fraction".
precise: fl(x op y) = (x op y)(1 + δ) with |δ| ≤ u for op ∈ {+, −, ×, ÷} (and square root), provided no overflow or underflow occurs; it follows from correct rounding (F0-73).
source: B1 of F0-74 (Nicholas J. Higham, "Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms" (SIAM; tier 3) — title only, not opened); S1 of F0-74 (IEEE, "IEEE Standard for Floating-Point Arithmetic" (IEEE Std 754; tier 1) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how far off an answer is, in its own units or as a fraction of the true value.
analogy: "two grams too much" versus "two grams in a kilogram".
precise: for an approximation x̂ of x: absolute error |x̂ − x|; relative error |x̂ − x| / |x| (for x ≠ 0). Floating point controls relative error.
source: B1 of F0-74 (Nicholas J. Higham, "Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms" (SIAM; tier 3) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the roundings of many operations adding up.
analogy: a thousand scoops' small spills.
precise: after k dependent roundings the relative error is bounded by γ_k = ku / (1 − ku) (for ku < 1); the bound grows linearly with k, while measured errors are often smaller because roundings partly cancel.
source: B1 of F0-74 (Nicholas J. Higham, "Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms" (SIAM; tier 3) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: adding numbers one after another into one running total.
analogy: Hana's single jar.
precise: s_0 = 0, s_k = fl(s_k−1 + x_k); the first input passes through n − 1 roundings, so |error| ≤ γ_n−1 Σ|x_i|.
source: B1 of F0-75 (Nicholas J. Higham, "Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms" (SIAM; tier 3) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: adding neighbours in pairs, then pairs of pairs, until one number is left.
analogy: Jamal's piles of piles.
precise: a balanced binary tree of additions with depth ⌈log_2 n⌉, so |error| ≤ γ_⌈log2 n⌉ Σ|x_i|.
source: B1 of F0-75 (Nicholas J. Higham, "Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms" (SIAM; tier 3) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the largest number of additions any one input goes through.
analogy: how many times the first coin was re-counted on its way to the total.
precise: the length of the longest path from an input to the result in the tree of additions; every order satisfies |error| ≤ γ_depth Σ|x_i| (this course's working rule, from the bound per input in B1).
source: B1 of F0-75 (Nicholas J. Higham, "Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms" (SIAM; tier 3) — title only, not opened); D1 of F0-75 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a running sum that also keeps track of what each addition rounded away and puts it back.
analogy: Amara's notepad of crumbs.
precise: keeps a correction c: y = x_k − c; t = s + y; c = (t − s) − y; s = t. Its error is bounded by (2u + O(nu^2)) Σ|x_i|, nearly independent of n.
source: B1 of F0-75 (Nicholas J. Higham, "Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms" (SIAM; tier 3) — title only, not opened); S2 of F0-75 (David Goldberg, "What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic" (ACM Computing Surveys, 1991; tier 5) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how much a sum magnifies small relative changes in its terms.
analogy: counting the coins of two people who owe each other almost the same amount: a tiny counting slip is a big part of the small difference.
precise: κ = Σ|x_i| / |Σx_i|; relative errors of order u in the terms can produce a relative error of order κu in the sum. κ = 1 for terms of one sign.
source: B1 of F0-75 (Nicholas J. Higham, "Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms" (SIAM; tier 3) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the largest difference from the reference that a test accepts, with a reason for its size.
analogy: "the count may be off by at most the crumbs of 166 scoops", not "off by a bit".
precise: a bound tol(n, data) derived from the computation's error analysis (for example γ_depth Σ|x_i| plus the reference's own error), such that a correct implementation can never exceed it and a wrong one usually does. The SP101 entry "Floating-point tolerance" is the general idea; this chapter makes its size derivable.
source: B1 of F0-75 (Nicholas J. Higham, "Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms" (SIAM; tier 3) — title only, not opened); U1 of F0-75 (this repository's curriculum or authoring guide: a map, not a source) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a rule that says how fast the state changes, plus where it starts.
analogy: "the hallway points this way here" and "you start at the sofa".
precise: x′(t) = f(t, x(t)), x(t_0) = x_0, where x is a vector (for a pendulum: angle θ and angular velocity ω); higher derivatives are turned into extra components (MA301 F0-67).
source: B2 of F0-76 (Ernst Hairer, Syvert P. Nørsett, Gerhard Wanner, "Solving Ordinary Differential Equations I: Nonstiff Problems" (Springer; tier 3) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how far forward in time a simulator jumps at once.
analogy: the length of Kenji's stride.
precise: the increment h = t_n+1 − t_n of a one-step method x_n+1 = x_n + h Φ(t_n, x_n, h).
source: B2 of F0-76 (Ernst Hairer, Syvert P. Nørsett, Gerhard Wanner, "Solving Ordinary Differential Equations I: Nonstiff Problems" (Springer; tier 3) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: move along today's direction for the whole step.
analogy: Kenji's first plan.
precise: x_n+1 = x_n + h f(t_n, x_n); a first-order method.
source: B2 of F0-76 (Ernst Hairer, Syvert P. Nørsett, Gerhard Wanner, "Solving Ordinary Differential Equations I: Nonstiff Problems" (Springer; tier 3) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
related: Discretisation rule (forward Euler, backward Euler, Tustin)

simple: update the velocity first, then move the position with the new velocity.
analogy: turn first, then step.
precise: for x′ = v, v′ = a(x): v_n+1 = v_n + h a(x_n), x_n+1 = x_n + h v_n+1; first order, and symplectic for mechanical systems of this form, which keeps the energy error bounded over long times.
source: B3 of F0-76 (Ernst Hairer, Christian Lubich, Gerhard Wanner, "Geometric Numerical Integration: Structure-Preserving Algorithms for Ordinary Differential Equations" (Springer; tier 3) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: look at the direction several times inside a step and average.
analogy: Kenji's peeks along the hallway.
precise: the classical fourth-order method: k_1 = f(t, x), k_2 = f(t + h/2, x + (h/2)k_1), k_3 = f(t + h/2, x + (h/2)k_2), k_4 = f(t + h, x + h k_3), x_n+1 = x_n + (h/6)(k_1 + 2k_2 + 2k_3 + k_4).
source: B2 of F0-76 (Ernst Hairer, Syvert P. Nørsett, Gerhard Wanner, "Solving Ordinary Differential Equations I: Nonstiff Problems" (Springer; tier 3) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

term: Order of accuracy (local and global truncation error)
simple: how fast a method's error shrinks when you shrink the step.
analogy: halve the stride: does Kenji end half as far off, or sixteen times closer?
precise: a method has order p if its local error per step is O(h^(p+1)) and its global error at a fixed end time is O(h^p); halving h divides the global error by about 2^p. Euler: p = 1; RK4: p = 4.
source: B2 of F0-76 (Ernst Hairer, Syvert P. Nørsett, Gerhard Wanner, "Solving Ordinary Differential Equations I: Nonstiff Problems" (Springer; tier 3) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: several equations, each a weighted sum of the same unknowns.
analogy: the receipts, with the prices unknown.
precise: Ax = b with A an n × n matrix, b a known vector and x the unknown vector; it has exactly one solution when A is nonsingular (det A ≠ 0).
source: B4 of F0-77 (Gilbert Strang, "Introduction to Linear Algebra" (tier 3; registry 4.2 for MA201) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: subtract multiples of one equation from the others until each equation has fewer unknowns.
analogy: using Kenji's receipt to remove apples from the others.
precise: for k = 1 … n−1, subtract l_ik = a_ik/a_kk times row k from each row i > k, producing an upper triangular system Ux = c, then solve it by back substitution from the last row up.
source: B2 of F0-77 (Lloyd N. Trefethen, David Bau III, "Numerical Linear Algebra" (SIAM; tier 3) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the number you divide by at each step, and the rule of picking the biggest one available.
analogy: the apple count on the receipt you work with.
precise: the pivot of step k is a_kk at that moment; partial pivoting first swaps row k with the row i ≥ k whose |a_ik| is largest, so every multiplier satisfies |l_ik| ≤ 1.
source: B2 of F0-77 (Lloyd N. Trefethen, David Bau III, "Numerical Linear Algebra" (SIAM; tier 3) — title only, not opened); B1 of F0-77 (Nicholas J. Higham, "Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms" (SIAM; tier 3) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: elimination written down so it can be reused for new right-hand sides.
analogy: keeping a note of every "subtract a quarter of Kenji's receipt" so that tomorrow's receipts with the same items take only seconds.
precise: PA = LU with P a permutation matrix (the row swaps), L unit lower triangular (the multipliers) and U upper triangular; then Ax = b is solved by Ly = Pb and Ux = y.
source: B2 of F0-77 (Lloyd N. Trefethen, David Bau III, "Numerical Linear Algebra" (SIAM; tier 3) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how far the answer fails to satisfy the equations.
analogy: put the computed prices back into the receipts and see by how much the totals are off.
precise: r = b − A x̂ for a computed x̂. A small residual means x̂ exactly solves a nearby problem; it does not by itself mean x̂ is close to x (F0-78).
source: B1 of F0-77 (Nicholas J. Higham, "Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms" (SIAM; tier 3) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the computed answer is the exact answer to a slightly changed question.
analogy: the prices you found are exactly right for receipts that differ from yours by a crumb.
precise: an algorithm for Ax = b is backward stable if its x̂ satisfies (A + ΔA) x̂ = b with ‖ΔA‖/‖A‖ of order the unit roundoff u; Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting has this property in practice, with a factor called the growth factor.
source: B1 of F0-77 (Nicholas J. Higham, "Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms" (SIAM; tier 3) — title only, not opened); B2 of F0-77 (Lloyd N. Trefethen, David Bau III, "Numerical Linear Algebra" (SIAM; tier 3) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how much a problem magnifies small changes in its input.
analogy: how far the cup tips per gram of finger pressure on the table.
precise: the relative condition number of y = f(x) is the limit of (relative change of y)/(relative change of x) for small changes; for differentiable scalar f, κ = |x f′(x)/f(x)|. It belongs to the problem, whatever algorithm is used.
source: B1 of F0-78 (Nicholas J. Higham, "Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms" (SIAM; tier 3) — title only, not opened); B2 of F0-78 (Lloyd N. Trefethen, David Bau III, "Numerical Linear Algebra" (SIAM; tier 3) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the condition number of solving Ax = b.
analogy: the wobble factor of a table built from the matrix.
precise: κ(A) = ‖A‖ ‖A^(−1)‖ in a chosen norm (κ_∞, κ_2); κ_2 = σ_max/σ_min, the ratio of the largest to the smallest singular value. κ ≥ 1, and κ = ∞ for a singular matrix.
source: B2 of F0-78 (Lloyd N. Trefethen, David Bau III, "Numerical Linear Algebra" (SIAM; tier 3) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how wrong the answer is, and how much you would have to change the question for the answer to be exactly right.
analogy: how far the cup is from where it should be, and how much the table would have to move for that to be its right place.
precise: for computed ŷ ≈ f(x): forward error |ŷ − f(x)|/|f(x)|; backward error the smallest |Δx|/|x| with ŷ = f(x + Δx).
source: B1 of F0-78 (Nicholas J. Higham, "Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms" (SIAM; tier 3) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an algorithm that adds no more error than rounding the input would.
analogy: a careful carrier.
precise: an algorithm is backward stable if its result is the exact answer for an input changed by a relative amount of order the unit roundoff u; then forward error ≲ κ × u.
source: B1 of F0-78 (Nicholas J. Higham, "Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms" (SIAM; tier 3) — title only, not opened); B2 of F0-78 (Lloyd N. Trefethen, David Bau III, "Numerical Linear Algebra" (SIAM; tier 3) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a problem whose answer is very sensitive to its data.
analogy: the wobbly table.
precise: a problem with κ large compared with 1/(required relative accuracy); with κ ≈ 10^k, expect to lose about k decimal digits of the input's accuracy, whatever the algorithm.
source: B1 of F0-78 (Nicholas J. Higham, "Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms" (SIAM; tier 3) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how often the controller looks and acts.
analogy: the time between Kenji's looks at the thermometer.
precise: the time T between successive executions of a discrete controller; the sampling rate is 1/T. Measurements y[k] = y(kT) and outputs u[k] are indexed by the sample number k.
source: B1 of F0-79 (Karl Johan Åström, Björn Wittenmark, "Computer-Controlled Systems: Theory and Design" (tier 3) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
related: Discretisation rule (forward Euler, backward Euler, Tustin)

simple: keep the output constant until the next update.
analogy: the tap stays where Kenji left it.
precise: u(t) = u[k] for kT ≤ t < (k+1)T; implemented by a DAC or PWM register written once per period. Combined with the sampler it adds a delay of about T/2 to the loop.
source: B1 of F0-79 (Karl Johan Åström, Björn Wittenmark, "Computer-Controlled Systems: Theory and Design" (tier 3) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
related: Discretisation rule (forward Euler, backward Euler, Tustin)

simple: the discrete version of a differential equation: the next value from the last few.
analogy: "turn the tap by this much, given what the thermometer said now and last time".
precise: a recurrence such as u[k] = u[k−1] + q_0e[k] + q_1e[k−1]; its transfer function in the variable z (one-sample shift) plays the role that s plays for differential equations.
source: B1 of F0-79 (Karl Johan Åström, Björn Wittenmark, "Computer-Controlled Systems: Theory and Design" (tier 3) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
related: Discretisation rule (forward Euler, backward Euler, Tustin)

term: Discretisation rule (forward Euler, backward Euler, Tustin)
simple: a recipe for replacing derivatives and integrals by sums and differences of samples.
analogy: different ways of estimating "how much water has flowed" from occasional looks.
precise: forward Euler s → (z − 1)/T, backward Euler s → (z − 1)/(zT), Tustin (bilinear, trapezoidal) s → (2/T)(z − 1)/(z + 1). For an integral these are the left rectangle, right rectangle and trapezoid rules.
source: B1 of F0-79 (Karl Johan Åström, Björn Wittenmark, "Computer-Controlled Systems: Theory and Design" (tier 3) — title only, not opened); D1 of F0-79 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the number that each step multiplies a disturbance by.
analogy: if every look-and-turn leaves the bath error at 0.8 of what it was, the error dies out; at −1.2, it flips and grows.
precise: a root z of the denominator of a discrete transfer function; a linear discrete system is stable when every pole has |z| < 1. A continuous pole s maps to z = e^sT under exact sampling.
source: B1 of F0-79 (Karl Johan Åström, Björn Wittenmark, "Computer-Controlled Systems: Theory and Design" (tier 3) — title only, not opened); B2 of F0-79 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" (tier 3; registry 4.2 for RB202, RB402, MA301) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: 8-bit floating-point formats, with either more precision (E4M3) or more range (E5M2).
analogy: the toy scoop set: a handful of marks per scoop.
precise: 1 sign bit, then 4 exponent and 3 fraction bits (E4M3) or 5 and 2 (E5M2); unit roundoff 2^(−4) and 2^(−3). The exact special values and largest number are set by the format's specification, not by IEEE 754 (Hardware section).
source: S2 of F0-80 (Open Compute Project, "OCP 8-bit Floating Point Specification (OFP8) — title only, not opened); S3 of F0-80 (Paulius Micikevicius and others, "FP8 Formats for Deep Learning" (2022; tier 5) — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the precision in which a sum or dot product keeps its running total.
analogy: whether Amara's running total is written on a coarse scoop or in her notebook.
precise: the format of the partial sums s_i = s_i−1 + a_ib_i; with k terms, its contribution to the error is bounded by γ_k(u_acc) Σ|a_ib_i| (F0-75), and the bound says nothing once k u_acc ≥ 1.
source: B1 of F0-80 (Nicholas J. Higham, "Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms" (SIAM; tier 3) — title only, not opened); D1 of F0-80 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the error made by storing the data in a short format before any arithmetic.
analogy: the coarse scoop itself.
precise: replacing a_i, b_i by fl(a_i), fl(b_i) with relative errors ≤ u_in changes each product by at most (2u_in + u_in^2)|a_ib_i|; no accumulator can remove it.
source: D1 of F0-80 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a list of every source of error with a bound for each, added up into a tolerance.
analogy: "scoops: at most this much; adding up: at most that much; the reference itself: a crumb".
precise: tolerance = Σ (bound of each independent error source), each term derived from u of the format involved, the problem's size and conditioning (Σ|x|), and the reference's own error.
source: D1 of F0-80 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); U1 of F0-80 (this repository's curriculum or authoring guide: a map, not a source) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a deliberately broken version that the test must reject.
analogy: before trusting the kitchen scale, put a known weight on it.
precise: a planted fault (an off-by-one, a dropped tail) run through the same test; if the test still passes, its tolerance or its inputs are too weak to detect faults of that size.
source: D1 of F0-80 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
